title: do something for someone with no receipt
hook: do something for someone with no receipt
tomorrow: you get one life and it ends

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: walking. Your line: walk someone home. Who did you keep company, even by a message? Day thirteen.

Be honest. When you do something nice, part of you keeps a little receipt. I drove them to the airport. I remembered her birthday. I did the dishes, again. Nobody's a saint about this; the receipts just print themselves. And sometimes we even want the other person to see the receipt. A thank-you, a mention, a like. Today's hook is a small experiment against that. Do something for someone, and make sure there's no receipt: no thanks, no credit, maybe nobody even knowing it was you. Today's word is service.
screen: `THE RECEIPT PRINTS ITSELF.` → `A THANK-YOU, A MENTION, A LIKE.` → `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus talks about giving to the poor, and says to do it so quietly that, in the King James wording, you "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Your own other hand shouldn't find out. In the twelfth century, the Jewish scholar Maimonides set out eight levels of giving, from grudging to generous. Near the very top: the giver and the receiver don't know each other's names. And at the top itself: helping someone so they won't need help again, a loan, a partnership, a job. In Sikh tradition the word is seva, selfless service, and you can see it in every gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship. Each one runs a langar, a free kitchen where anyone, of any faith or none, sits and eats together. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the kitchen feeds a vast number of people every day, and most of the hands doing it belong to people whose names nobody there will ever learn. And the Bhagavad Gita, in Hindu tradition, teaches acting without clinging to the fruits of the action: do the work well, and let go of what it earns you. Four homes, four reasons. Some serve because God sees what's hidden. Some because the other person's dignity matters. Some because the self gets smaller when it isn't keeping score. They don't mean the same thing by it. But each of them treats the receipt as the part to throw away.
screen: `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.` · `MAIMONIDES' LADDER OF GIVING.` · `SEVA AND THE FREE KITCHEN.` · `LET GO OF THE FRUITS.` · then, large: `THROW AWAY THE RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next forty-five seconds, think of one small thing you could do today for someone, where nobody would know it was you. Put a shopping cart back. Refill the coffee. Leave a kind review. Pay for something quietly. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it and walking away, no thank-you. Notice what that feels like. The bell holds the time.
Service. Doing good for someone else, without keeping the receipt. Thirteenth word.
Your line: no receipt. Today, do the thing you picked. Then don't mention it. Not to them, not to anyone. Tomorrow's the end of week two. Day thirteen.

screen: `DAY 13 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU GET ONE LIFE AND IT ENDS.`

howItsDone: Service is part of daily life in many traditions: Sikhs volunteer in the langar, the free kitchen of every gurdwara; many Christians and Jews give anonymously; and Hindus speak of acting without attachment to reward.

original.note: Gurmukhi, from Sikh tradition: selfless service, done without seeking reward. The word is also Sanskrit (सेवा).

trapdoor: what you thought: being useful, or volunteering now and then.
what it means: doing good for someone without keeping the receipt: no thanks, no credit.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14, ranks eight levels of tzedakah; the top is making the poor person self-sufficient.

sources.quoted: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14

notes: Maimonides' eight levels: top is strengthening the poor person's hand by gift, loan, partnership or work so they need no charity; second is giver and receiver unknown to each other. Confirm 'near the very top'.
Golden Temple langar numbers are often reported as 50,000–100,000 a day; the script says only 'a vast number'.
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 paraphrased (action without attachment to its fruits). A Hindu Keeper may refine.
The closing summary of reasons (God sees what's hidden; dignity; the self gets smaller) is attributed generally, not to specific traditions one-to-one, so as not to flatten any of them.
